title: THE ANGEL WHO SPOKE AS GOD: WAS JESUS WALKING THROUGH THE OLD TESTAMENT BEFORE BETHLEHEM?
paragraphs: THE ANGEL WHO SPOKE AS GOD: WAS JESUS WALKING THROUGH THE OLD TESTAMENT BEFORE BETHLEHEM?

The burning bush. The terrified warrior. The mysterious Messenger who accepted God's name, spoke with God's authority, and left men trembling in His presence. What if these ancient encounters were pointing toward the greatest revelation in human history—Jesus Christ Himself?
There is something deeply unsettling about the burning bush.
Not because it was burning.
But because Someone was speaking from inside the fire.
And the man standing before it had absolutely no idea how dramatically his life was about to change.
Moses wasn't standing inside a temple. He wasn't leading a worship service. He wasn't expecting a supernatural visitation.
He was tending sheep.
A former prince of Egypt, now living in the wilderness, carrying a past stained by bloodshed, failure, fear, and exile.
Forty years earlier, Moses had killed an Egyptian and fled for his life (Exodus 2:11–15; Acts 7:23–30).
Perhaps he thought the most significant chapter of his life was already behind him.
Then he saw something that should have been impossible.
A bush engulfed in flames.
Yet the branches weren't turning to ashes.
The fire burned, but the bush was not consumed.
Moses moved closer.
And then a voice called his name.
"Moses, Moses."
He answered, "Here am I."
But what happened next reveals one of the most astonishing mysteries woven throughout the Old Testament.
Because Exodus doesn't initially say that God appeared in the bush.
It says something far more intriguing.
"And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush." — Exodus 3:2, KJV
The Angel of the LORD.
But just two verses later, the same passage declares:
"God called unto him out of the midst of the bush." — Exodus 3:4, KJV
And then the voice identifies Himself:
"I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." — Exodus 3:6, KJV
Read that carefully.
The Angel of the LORD appears.
God speaks.
And the One speaking identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Moses doesn't respond as though he has encountered an ordinary angel delivering a heavenly message.
Scripture says he hides his face because he is afraid to look upon God.
Who was this mysterious Messenger?
And why does His identity matter so profoundly for understanding Jesus Christ?
Because this question takes us beyond a burning bush, beyond a frightened man hiding in a winepress, and into the astonishing unity of God's redemptive story.
A story that begins long before Bethlehem.
A story that reaches its climax at Calvary.
A story in which the God who calls sinners out of hiding is the same God who provides their salvation.
And perhaps, before we reach the end, you'll recognize something painfully familiar about the people He chose to visit.
Because Moses wasn't looking for a second chance.
Gideon wasn't looking for a confrontation with heaven.
And many of us aren't prepared for what happens when God's Word exposes the places where we've been hiding.
But first, we need to understand who this Angel actually was.
In the Hebrew text of Exodus 3:2, the expression is:
מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה — malʾakh YHWH
It means "messenger of the LORD" or "angel of the LORD."
The Hebrew word malʾakh describes a messenger. Depending on the context, that messenger may be human or heavenly.
The word itself does not automatically tell us the messenger's nature.
It describes the messenger's function.
That distinction is enormously important.
Because when modern readers hear "angel," they often immediately picture a created heavenly being.
But the Hebrew term does not, by itself, establish that conclusion.
We have to examine what the Messenger says, what He does, how Scripture describes Him, and how the passage fits within the Bible's wider revelation.
And this is where the mystery deepens.
In Exodus 3, the Messenger is introduced as the Angel of the LORD, yet the narrative identifies the speaker as God.
When Moses asks for His name, the answer comes:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה — ʾehyeh ʾasher ʾehyeh
Traditionally rendered:
"I AM THAT I AM." — Exodus 3:14, KJV
The Hebrew expression can also be understood as "I AM WHO I AM" or "I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE," reflecting the richness of the Hebrew verb for being.
This is no ordinary introduction.
The One speaking reveals Himself as the covenant God who will be faithful to His promises and present with His people.
And notice what He does not say.
He doesn't say Moses has become too old.
He doesn't say his previous failure has permanently disqualified him.
He doesn't pretend Moses' past never happened, either.
Instead, He calls Moses into a mission far greater than Moses' confidence or ability.
When Moses objects, "Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?" God's answer is not a speech about Moses' hidden greatness.
It is a promise.
"Certainly I will be with thee." — Exodus 3:12, KJV
There it is.
The foundation of Moses' calling was never Moses' worthiness.
It was God's presence.
And someone reading this needs to understand the difference.
Your failures are real.
Your sins cannot be excused.
Your past may have consequences you still carry.
But your history does not place you beyond the reach of God's mercy.
Repentance is not pretending the past never happened.
Grace is not God declaring evil harmless.
Grace is God doing for sinners what they could never accomplish through their own righteousness.
And ultimately, that grace is revealed through Jesus Christ.
But the burning bush isn't the only place where this mysterious Angel appears.
Centuries later, another man encounters Him.
And this time, the man isn't standing before a burning bush.
He's hiding.
His name is Gideon.
Israel has fallen into a devastating cycle of disobedience, oppression, desperation, and crying out to God.
The Midianites have ravaged the land.
Israel's crops have been destroyed or seized.
The people have been driven into hiding.
And Gideon is threshing wheat in a winepress, trying to conceal what little food he can preserve.
Then Scripture says:
"And the angel of the LORD came, and sat under an oak which was in Ophrah." — Judges 6:11, KJV
Imagine that scene.
A frightened man trying to survive.
Dust on his clothes.
An uncertain future.
The crushing weight of an occupied nation.
And a heavenly Messenger sitting beneath a tree.
Then comes a greeting that must have sounded almost absurd.
"The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." — Judges 6:12, KJV
Mighty man of valor?
Gideon is hiding from his enemies.
He isn't standing on a battlefield.
He isn't commanding an army.
He isn't demonstrating heroic courage.
He is trying not to be discovered.
And yet the Messenger addresses him in terms of the calling God is placing upon him.
But Gideon doesn't immediately respond with triumphant faith.
He responds with a question that sounds painfully human.
"If the LORD be with us, why then is all this befallen us?" — Judges 6:13, KJV
Have you ever prayed something similar?
If God is with me, why is my family falling apart?
If God hears me, why does this suffering continue?
If God is faithful, why do I feel abandoned?
Gideon's question comes from a nation experiencing genuine suffering, though Judges also explains that Israel's covenant unfaithfulness contributed to its condition.
The text does not dismiss the suffering.
Neither does it excuse the sin.
It brings both into the presence of God.
And then something extraordinary happens.
Judges 6:14 says:
"And the LORD looked upon him, and said, Go in this thy might." — KJV
Did you notice the transition?
The Angel of the LORD appears in verse 11.
The Angel speaks in verse 12.
But in verse 14, the narrative says the LORD Himself looks at Gideon and speaks.
The Hebrew uses the divine name YHWH.
The same covenant name associated with the God who called Moses.
And when Gideon protests that his family is poor and that he is the least in his father's house, the answer echoes the burning bush.
"Surely I will be with thee." — Judges 6:16, KJV
Different man.
Different generation.
Different crisis.
The same divine assurance.
God's presence is greater than the weakness of the person He calls.
But Gideon's encounter becomes even more startling.
He prepares an offering of meat, unleavened cakes, and broth.
The Angel instructs him to place the meat and bread upon a rock and pour out the broth.
Then the Angel touches the offering with the end of His staff.
Fire rises from the rock and consumes it.
And the Angel of the LORD disappears.
Gideon suddenly understands the terrifying significance of what he has witnessed.
"Alas, O Lord GOD! for because I have seen an angel of the LORD face to face." — Judges 6:22, KJV
Gideon fears death.
Yet the LORD answers:
"Peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die." — Judges 6:23, KJV
So Gideon builds an altar and calls it Jehovah-shalom.
The LORD is peace.
And now the question becomes impossible to ignore.
Why do these encounters repeatedly move between the Angel of the LORD and the LORD Himself?
Why does the Messenger sometimes speak as God, rather than merely delivering a message from God?
And could these appearances have anything to do with Jesus?
Here we must be careful.
Not because the question is unimportant.
But because Scripture deserves more than sensational conclusions.
Many Christians throughout church history have understood certain appearances of the Angel of the LORD as preincarnate appearances of the Son of God.
The theological term is Christophany—an appearance of Christ before His incarnation.
This interpretation is especially associated with passages in which the Angel of the LORD speaks with divine authority, bears the divine name, or is identified with God in the surrounding narrative.
It is a serious, historically influential Christian interpretation.
But it is important to state something clearly.
Exodus 3 and Judges 6 do not explicitly identify the Angel of the LORD as Jesus Christ.

Other interpreters understand these passages through the biblical principle of divine agency: God's messenger may speak on God's behalf so fully that the narrative moves between the messenger and the God who sent him.
That explanation also deserves consideration.
And the New Testament does not provide a single, unambiguous statement saying, "The Angel of the LORD in Exodus 3 and Judges 6 was Jesus."
We should not claim that it does.
Faithfulness to Scripture means distinguishing between what the Bible explicitly teaches and what Christians reasonably infer from its wider testimony.
But there are powerful reasons why Christians have connected these mysterious appearances with the eternal Son.
John's Gospel opens with words that take us back before creation itself.
"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." — John 1:1, KJV
The Greek reads:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος — En archē ēn ho logos
"In the beginning was the Word."
And later:
καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος — kai theos ēn ho logos
"And the Word was God."
John does not present Jesus as a created being who began existing in Bethlehem.
He presents the Word as eternally existing, personally distinct from the Father, and truly divine.
Then John 1:14 announces:
"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." — KJV
The eternal Son entered human history by taking on human nature.
Bethlehem was not the beginning of His existence.
It was the beginning of His incarnate earthly life.
And that distinction changes how Christians read the Old Testament.
Because the Son did not begin to exist when Mary gave birth.
He was already eternal.
He was already divine.
He was already active in God's works.
Colossians 1:16–17 teaches that all things were created through Christ and for Him, and that He is before all things.
Hebrews 1:1–3 presents the Son as the One through whom God made the worlds and as the radiance of God's glory.
And John 1:18 describes the unique role of the Son in making God known.
These passages establish the eternal identity and divine activity of Christ.
They make the possibility of preincarnate appearances theologically coherent.
They do not, by themselves, prove that every Old Testament appearance of the Angel of the LORD was Christ.
But they reveal why the question matters.
The Jesus revealed in the New Testament is not an afterthought in God's plan.
He is the eternal Son through whom God's saving purposes reach their fulfillment.
And then we come to another extraordinary connection.
In John 8, Jesus confronts religious opponents who challenge His claims.
The conversation turns to Abraham.
And Jesus declares:
"Before Abraham was, I am." — John 8:58, KJV
In Greek:
πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι ἐγὼ εἰμί — prin Abraam genesthai egō eimi
Notice the contrast.
Abraham came into existence.
Jesus says, "I am."
The wording is striking.
Many Christian interpreters understand this as an assertion of Christ's eternal existence and divine identity, with an important theological connection to God's self-revelation in Exodus.
The surrounding narrative shows how seriously His opponents took the statement: they picked up stones to throw at Him.
We should also recognize that the Greek expression egō eimi does not always function as a divine-name declaration in every context.
And the Greek translation of Exodus 3:14 has its own distinctive wording.
The connection between these passages is therefore theological and contextual, not simply a claim that the Hebrew and Greek phrases are identical.
But the larger testimony of John's Gospel is unmistakable.
Jesus is not merely a prophet telling people about God.
He is the eternal Word who became flesh.
He is the Son who reveals the Father.
He is worthy of the honor due to God.
And He is the One through whom salvation comes.
Now think again about Moses.
A man burdened by failure, standing barefoot before holy ground.
Think about Gideon.
A frightened man hiding from his enemies, overwhelmed by the weakness of his own circumstances.
Neither man could save his people by personal strength.
Both needed God's presence.
Both needed God's promise.
Both were confronted by the holiness of the One who called them.
And both stories ultimately belong to the larger biblical account of God's faithfulness.
But there is another truth we must not miss.
The Angel of the LORD is not always presented in exactly the same way in every Old Testament passage.
Sometimes the language strongly identifies the Messenger with God.
Elsewhere the distinction between God and His messenger is more apparent.
The term itself does not guarantee that every occurrence refers to the same kind of manifestation.
That is why careful interpretation examines each passage rather than forcing every reference into a single conclusion.
Consider another important encounter.
In Genesis 16, Hagar is fleeing into the wilderness.
She is an Egyptian servant who has suffered mistreatment and finds herself vulnerable and alone.
The Angel of the LORD meets her.
The narrative describes the encounter in language that leads Hagar to speak of the LORD who has seen her.
She calls Him El Roi, commonly understood as "the God who sees me."
Here again, God's revelation reaches someone living at the margins.
Someone whose pain others might have ignored.
Someone whose future seemed uncertain.
And whether one understands this appearance as a Christophany or as God speaking through His messenger, the passage reveals something precious and undeniable.
The living God sees the afflicted.
He is not indifferent to suffering.
He is not unaware of the wilderness.
But the full revelation of God's mercy does not stop with Hagar, Moses, or Gideon.
It leads us to Jesus.
And here the mystery becomes personal.
Because there is a danger in becoming so fascinated by the identity of the Angel of the LORD that we miss the central message of Scripture.
We can study Hebrew vocabulary.
We can compare Greek expressions.
We can debate ancient appearances.
We can learn the vocabulary of theology.
And still avoid the question that matters most.
Have you actually surrendered your life to the Jesus whom Scripture reveals?
Not merely admired Him.
Not simply agreed that He exists.
Not merely shared Christian posts or attended church.
Have you turned to Him in repentance and faith?
Because the God who spoke from the burning bush is holy.
And holiness is not something sinful humanity can casually approach on its own terms.
When Moses draws near, he is commanded to remove his shoes.
The ground is holy because God has manifested His presence there.
Moses hides his face.
Gideon fears that he will die.
These are not scenes designed to make God appear harmless.
They confront us with the majesty of the Creator.
And yet, in the fullness of time, the eternal Son truly became man.
He entered a world filled with rebellion, violence, hypocrisy, grief, and shame.
He walked among sinners.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the repentant.
He confronted religious pride.
He called people out of darkness.
He exposed sin without becoming a sinner.
He loved without compromising truth.
And then He went to the cross.
Not because humanity was innocent.
But because humanity was guilty.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because sin was so serious that our redemption required the sacrifice of the spotless Lamb of God.
At Calvary, Jesus bore the judgment due to sinners, fulfilling God's saving purpose through His atoning death.
And on the third day, He rose bodily from the dead.
This is the Gospel.
Not a motivational speech about becoming a better version of yourself.
Not a promise that following Jesus will eliminate every hardship.
Not a religious system in which you purchase God's acceptance through good deeds.
It is the good news that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And salvation is received by God's grace through faith, not earned through human achievement (Ephesians 2:8–9).
That means you cannot buy forgiveness.
You cannot earn redemption through donations.
And no financial contribution, however generous, can replace repentance and faith in Christ.
Jesus has already accomplished what money could never purchase.
But those who have received His grace are called to respond with grateful obedience, love, generosity, and a desire to make the Gospel known.
And that is where this message reaches beyond ancient history.
Maybe you're reading this while carrying a secret nobody knows.
Maybe your family thinks you're spiritually strong, but you know how exhausted you've become.
Maybe you've been hiding behind church attendance while privately wrestling with sin.
Maybe you love Jesus, but lately your prayers have felt empty.
Maybe you once walked closely with God, but compromise slowly became comfortable.
Or perhaps you don't yet believe, and you're wondering whether the God of the Bible could possibly care about someone like you.
Look again at Moses.
Look again at Gideon.
Their stories are not identical to yours.
And their specific callings were not promises that every believer will experience a burning bush or receive an extraordinary military commission.
But they reveal the character of a God who acts in history, confronts human weakness, calls people to trust Him, and remains faithful to His purposes.
And through Jesus Christ, we are invited to something even greater than witnessing a mysterious flame.
We are invited to be reconciled to God.
Not because we deserve it.
But because Christ is sufficient.
There is a line in Hebrews 1:1–2 that brings the entire discussion into focus.
God spoke in various ways through the prophets in former times.
But in these last days, He has spoken to us by His Son.
That is the decisive revelation.
Whatever conclusions Christians reach about particular appearances of the Angel of the LORD, we do not need to search for an uncertain manifestation to know what God is like.
We look to Jesus Christ.
He is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15).
He is the exact representation of God's nature (Hebrews 1:3).
He is the One who said, "He that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (John 14:9).
And He is the only mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5).
The burning bush makes us wonder.
The encounter with Gideon makes us tremble.
The Hebrew text makes us examine.
The New Testament makes us behold the eternal Son.
And the cross brings us to the point of decision.
What will you do with Jesus?
Because one day, the most important question will not be whether you correctly identified every mysterious Messenger in the Old Testament.
It will be whether you have placed your trust in the Savior whom the Scriptures proclaim.
And that question is too important to hide behind religious familiarity.
Maybe you've been saying, "I'll come back to God when I fix myself."
But you cannot cleanse your own heart by waiting.
Maybe you've been saying, "I've gone too far."
But the mercy of Christ is greater than the guilt of every sinner who truly comes to Him.
Maybe you've been saying, "I believe in God, so I'm fine."
But the Gospel calls us beyond vague belief into repentance and personal trust in Jesus Christ.
Hear His invitation:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." — John 6:37, KJV
That promise is not reserved for people with respectable histories.
It is for those who come to Christ.
Bring your guilt.
Bring your shame.
Bring the sins you've been defending.
Bring the fears you've been concealing.
Bring the questions you still struggle to answer.
You do not have to pretend to be righteous before coming to the Savior.
But you must not cling to sin as though it were more precious than Him.
Turn to Christ.
Trust His finished work.
Receive His mercy.
And follow Him.
If this message has exposed something you've been hiding, you can begin with a simple, sincere prayer:

"Lord Jesus, I confess that I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising from the dead. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You in truth. I surrender my life to You. Amen."
The prayer itself is not a magical formula.
It is the repentance and faith expressed from the heart that matter.
And if you're already a believer but have grown weary, remember this:
The Christian life is not sustained by pretending you are strong.
It is sustained by the grace of the Savior who remains faithful.
Now I want to ask you something personal.
When you read about Moses hiding his face and Gideon hiding in a winepress, which man did you recognize in yourself?
The person ashamed of the past?
Or the person frightened of the future?
Perhaps both.
You don't have to reveal private details or expose wounds you're not ready to discuss.
And if you've experienced God's restoration after a season of failure, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Your words may encourage someone who believes their story is already over.
Because sometimes a testimony becomes the reminder another believer desperately needed.

Return to Exodus 3:2–6, Judges 6:11–24, John 1:1–18, and Hebrews 1:1–3. Read them carefully. Examine the context. Let God's Word shape your convictions rather than relying on an emotional experience alone.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen.
But because someone in your circle may be wrestling with the very questions we have explored.
Someone may be spiritually exhausted.
Someone may have quietly walked away from church.
Someone may believe their past has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone may never have understood that Jesus Christ existed before Bethlehem.
One thoughtful share can place the Scriptures before a person you may never have known was searching.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture more deeply, understand the Gospel more clearly, and become more firmly rooted in Jesus Christ.
They are also part of a ministry mission that requires time, labor, resources, and ongoing support.
And that brings me to something I want to share with you openly.
And not because we can claim that God requires you to support this particular ministry.
Scripture makes no such demand.
But the Bible does encourage believers to support faithful Gospel ministry willingly, generously, and according to their means.
Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — KJV
And Philippians 4:15–18 shows believers participating in Gospel ministry through practical financial support.
It should never be treated as a compulsory tithe, a substitute for responsibilities to your local church, or a requirement for spiritual blessing.
Rather, it can be a voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in the Gospel.
Those items are simply expressions of appreciation.
They are not the heart of the mission.
The mission is Jesus Christ.
The mission is biblical truth.
The mission is helping people move beyond religious appearances into genuine repentance, faith, spiritual maturity, and transformation through the Gospel.
Pray for the ministry.
Read and share the Scriptures.
Encourage others to grow in Christ.
And if you have the desire and means to help sustain this work monthly, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
There is no pressure to give beyond your ability.
No promise that a payment will unlock a miracle.
Just an invitation to participate willingly in a ministry that desires to lift up the name of Jesus Christ.
Only Jesus saves.
And the greatest thing Gospel Warrior could ever accomplish is to help one more person hear His Word, understand His Gospel, and turn to Him in faith.
Picture Moses.
The sheep are nearby.
The desert is silent.
The bush is burning.
A voice calls his name.
He removes his sandals.
He hides his face.
And the God who remembers His covenant prepares to deliver His people.
Then picture Gideon.
A frightened man in a winepress.
A nation crushed by oppression.
A Messenger beneath an oak tree.
A promise of divine presence.
Fire rising from a rock.
And a trembling man hearing the words:
"Peace be unto thee."
We may continue studying the precise identity of these mysterious appearances, and faithful Christians may reach different conclusions about the Angel of the LORD.
But the greatest revelation is no longer hidden in a question about an ancient Messenger.
It has been made known in Jesus Christ.
The eternal Son came in the flesh.
The sinless Savior died for sinners.
The crucified Lord rose from the grave.
And everyone who truly trusts in Him receives the promise of salvation.
That is the hope Moses and Gideon could only anticipate within their own place in redemptive history.
That is the Gospel we now proclaim openly.
And that is the grace capable of rewriting a human story—not by erasing its history, but by redeeming the sinner and making all things new in Christ.
So if your life has become a wilderness, don't mistake the silence for proof that God has forgotten you.
If your heart has become a hiding place, don't confuse concealment with safety.
And if your past feels like a scandal that can never be overcome, remember that the cross declares both the seriousness of your sin and the astonishing sufficiency of your Savior.
The greatest wonder was never that God spoke from a burning bush—but that the eternal Son came into our broken world to bring sinners home to God.
